snapshot.title: SSC History: Modern India — Gandhian Era
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC History Hook: 1915: Gandhi. 1929: Purna Swaraj. 1930: Dandi. 1942: Quit India. Do or Die: 1942. Tilak: Swaraj.

quick_notes.title: Gandhi's Arrival
quick_notes.detail: 1915 from South Africa. Early struggles : Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), Ahmedabad (1918).
quick_notes.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in the year 1915. He then led his first major struggles in India to help poor farmers and workers. In 1917, he organized the Champaran Satyagraha in Bihar to protest against the forced growing of indigo by British planters on farmers' land. In 1918, he led the Kheda Satyagraha in Gujarat to support farmers who could not pay taxes due to crop failure and plague. Also in 1918, he led the Ahmedabad Mill Strike to support textile mill workers who were demanding a wage increase. These early movements established Gandhi's method of non-violent protest and made him a national leader.

quick_notes.title: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922)
quick_notes.detail: Withdrawn due to Chauri Chaura incident. Slogan : Swaraj in one year.
quick_notes.explanation: The Non-Cooperation Movement was a nationwide protest led by Mahatma Gandhi from 1920 to 1922, where Indians refused to cooperate with British rule by boycotting British goods, schools, courts, and government jobs. The main goal was to achieve Swaraj, which means self-rule or independence, and the popular slogan was "Swaraj in one year," meaning they hoped to win freedom within a year. The movement was suddenly withdrawn, or called off, by Gandhi in February 1922 because of the Chauri Chaura incident, where a violent mob set fire to a police station in the town of Chauri Chaura, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi believed that the movement had to be non-violent, and this act of violence went against his principle of ahimsa, or non-violence. As a result, the movement ended without achieving Swaraj, but it united many Indians in the struggle for freedom.

quick_notes.title: Civil Disobedience (1930)
quick_notes.detail: Started with Dandi March (6 April 1930). Salt Satyagraha. Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931).
quick_notes.explanation: Civil Disobedience is a form of peaceful protest where people deliberately break a law they believe is unjust, and accept the punishment without violence. This movement began with the Dandi March, a 24-day walk led by Mahatma Gandhi starting on 12 March 1930, which ended on 6 April 1930 when Gandhi broke the British salt law by making salt from seawater at Dandi. This specific act of breaking the salt law is called the Salt Satyagraha, where Satyagraha means a method of non-violent resistance or holding firmly to the truth. The movement continued until it was paused by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, signed in March 1931, which was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the British Viceroy of India, that ended the civil disobedience campaign in exchange for the release of political prisoners and the right to make salt for personal use.

quick_notes.title: Quit India Movement (1942)
quick_notes.detail: "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro). Launched on 8th August 1942 from Bombay.
quick_notes.explanation: The Quit India Movement was a major push for Indian independence from British rule, launched on 8th August 1942 from Bombay (now Mumbai). It was led by Mahatma Gandhi, who gave the slogan "Do or Die" (in Hindi, "Karo ya Maro"), meaning that Indians must either achieve freedom or give up their lives in the struggle. This movement called for the British to immediately leave India, and it involved mass protests, strikes, and civil disobedience across the country. The British government responded by arresting Gandhi and other leaders, but the movement spread widely and is a key step towards India’s independence in 1947.

quick_notes.title: Key Pacts & Sessions
quick_notes.detail: Lucknow Pact (1916). Lahore Session (1929 - Purna Swaraj). Poona Pact (1932 - Gandhi & Ambedkar).
quick_notes.explanation: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League where they decided to work together to ask the British for more self-rule for Indians. The Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in 1929 was the meeting where the Congress declared Purna Swaraj, which means complete and total independence from British rule, as their official goal. The Poona Pact of 1932 was an agreement between Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who represented the Depressed Classes (now called Scheduled Castes or SC), and Mahatma Gandhi, who was fasting in protest, to keep a single system of voting for all Hindus instead of creating separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

topic_title: SSC History: Modern India — Gandhian Era
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Mass Struggles'. The arrival of Gandhi changed the freedom movement from an elite debate to a common man's fight. We explore the 'Big Three'—Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Quit India. In SSC, the 'Years' and 'Pacts' (Gandhi-Irwin, Poona) are high-yield. Do you know who was called 'Frontier Gandhi'? Or which session demanded 'Purna Swaraj'? Let's finish the modern timeline today.
